item.title: Scalable Simulation of Quantum Dynamics on Topological Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Unitary propagators for real-time molecular and condensed-phase dynamics are synthesized via Solovay-Kitaev braiding of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, achieving an accuracy target of 10−8 across two-level, spin-boson, and molecular reaction systems.

Grade 0.412 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Kritanjan Polley, Mark E. Tuckerman

Figure

Population dynamics versus time for a two-level system under exact unitary evolution compared to Fibonacci and Ising anyon braiding sequences generated by the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm with 10−7 infidelity.

Asks

Can real-time quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems be represented and executed using non-Abelian anyon braiding on topological quantum hardware?

But

Classical digital simulation of anyon braiding circuits rather than execution on topological quantum hardware; requires probabilistic imaginary time evolution for thermal states.

Tools

Fibonacci and Ising anyon braiding · Solovay-Kitaev algorithm · Givens rotations · Tensor network path integrals · Probabilistic imaginary time evolution (PITE)

Abstract

Quantum computers offer a significant advantage in simulating quantum systems compared to classical computers for certain problems, although most current applications are limited to calculating static molecular properties using hybrid quantum-classical hardware. In this work, we establish a framework for the representation of quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems, designed for execution on topological quantum hardware. By leveraging the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, we utilize the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a range of systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms across a hierarchy of complexity, from two-level systems and one dimensional double-well potentials to condensed phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics. These algorithms provide a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

item.title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines architectural blueprint for utility-scale quantum systems treating QPUs as classical heterogeneous accelerators with specialized local hardware stacks for control, readout, and QEC below the ISA boundary.

Grade 0.399 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Torsten Hoefler, Matthias Troyer

Asks

How should utility-scale quantum computing systems be architected and integrated with classical compute to optimize cost-performance?

But

Architectural proposal and design blueprint; relies on scaling assumptions for physical qubit modalities and QEC decoding.

Tools

system architecture analysis · QEC integration models · classical accelerator design analogies

Abstract

Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

item.title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Realizes bounded finite impulse response (FIR) filtering on a quantum computer via a unitary state-space lattice decomposition without mid-circuit measurements or gain loss, demonstrated on N=32 samples with filter order M=12.

Grade 0.372 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Roope Salmi, Davide Rocchesso, Vesa Välimäki

Figure

Sample index n versus normalized amplitude for two parallel input signals (impulse x0(n) and fractal sequence x1(n), red) and their resulting lowpass filtered outputs (y0(n) and y1(n), blue), comparing exact statevector amplitudes with 1024-shot Hadamard test estimates.

Asks

How can discrete-time sample-based linear signal processing and FIR filters be implemented in a composable unitary quantum circuit without losing signal gain?

Before

In prior quantum FIR filters (Majumdar et al. 2021), input samples were consumed without reuse, preventing composability without intermediate classical conversion.

But

Simulated on ideal quantum simulator with 1024-shot sampling; requires known power complementary transfer function and large circuit depths (59,292 elementary gates for N=32,M=12) requiring fault-tolerant hardware.

Tools

Vaidyanathan unitary lattice filterbank decomposition · quantum delay and transposition gates · Hadamard test · Qiskit simulator

Code. https://github.com/ollpu/quantum-fir/

Abstract

Many signal processing tasks require intensive computations. Quantum computing promises to accelerate certain tasks, but algorithms must be designed around the limitations of quantum mechanics. This paper provides a quantum implementation of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, which are a widely used tool in classical signal processing. The filter can be parallelized and composed as part of larger quantum algorithms, with potential for speedups using quantum amplitude estimation and future fault-tolerant quantum hardware. To accomplish these properties, we introduce a state-space framework wherein sample-based signal processing is performed with unitary quantum circuits. We present the quantum delay gate as the quantum analog of the delay line in discrete-time signal processing. Unitary circuits intrinsically describe lossless systems, but we also implement lowpass and other bounded filters by emulating a projection operator. The FIR filter implementation is tested and demonstrated with a quantum circuit simulator.

item.title: Efficiently estimating failure rates of fault-tolerant logical non-Clifford blocks
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Efficient classical sampling and decoding success estimation for fault-tolerant third-order circuits (CSS operations plus diagonal gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy like T, CS, CCZ) with non-Clifford simulation overhead independent of logical qubit count.

Grade 0.368 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Thomas R. Scruby

Asks

How can the logical failure rate and decoding performance of fault-tolerant quantum circuits implementing non-Clifford gates be estimated efficiently?

But

Logical failure rate estimate is an overestimate. Efficient sampling requires combined X-like errors to satisfy a contractibility condition (Condition C); checking this condition exactly is exponentially hard in circuit volume without topological or geometric structure.

Tools

spacetime fault complex cohomology · twisted detector-error model · contractibility condition verification · Z₂ linear solvers · Pauli frame tracking

Abstract

Useful quantum computation requires the fault-tolerant implementations of a universal gate set which are generically not efficiently simulable. We devise an algebraic framework that allows for efficient sampling from the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits that implement diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy. Upon successful sampling we also provide sufficient conditions for decoding success. The resulting estimate for the logical failure rate is an overestimate, which becomes more accurate for blocks that are fault tolerant against arbitrary local errors. The non-Clifford simulation overhead is independent of the number of logical qubits, making the method particularly attractive for large-scale simulations. The framework is based on viewing the non-Clifford gates in the circuit as a cohomology invariant of an underlying spacetime fault complex. The method can also be interfaced with Clifford simulators to simulate larger fault-tolerant circuits and algorithmic subroutines.

item.title: Scalable logical qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines scalable logical qubits across four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance. Establishes criteria requiring repeated quantum error correction, low-latency real-time decoding/feedback, fault-tolerant universal operations, and replicability to hundreds or thousands of qubits.

Grade 0.367 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Matthias Troyer, Chetan Nayak, John Martinis

Asks

How can progress toward error-corrected logical qubits for utility-scale quantum computing be measured and compared systematically?

But

Conceptual/framework paper; relies on theoretical trade-offs across reliability, scale, capability, and performance rather than a specific experimental implementation.

Tools

quantum error correction · real-time syndrome decoding · fault-tolerant universal gate architectures

Abstract

Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

item.title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — The number of quantum measurement shots required to reconstruct NMR spectra at fixed accuracy scales sub-exponentially with spin-chain length L, showing a pronounced flattening for 1D and 2D molecular geometries with distance-decaying couplings up to L=50.

Grade 0.364 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Sebastian Walch, Keith R. Fratus, Jan-Michael Reiner, Igor Lesanovsky

Figure

Spectral infidelity versus system size L (at R=1024 shots) for 1D chains and four real molecules under full Heisenberg interactions, demonstrating weak growth with L.

Asks

How does the number of projective measurement shots required to compute NMR spectra to a given accuracy scale with the number of nuclear spins?

But

Low-field NMR setting only. All gate noise, decoherence, and Trotterization errors neglected (pure shot-noise limit). Full Heisenberg dynamics verified only up to L=12 and on four real molecules.

Tools

Exact diagonalization · Ising NMR toy Hamiltonian benchmark · Repeated-measurement shot-noise simulation · Fast Fourier transform (FFT)

Abstract

Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

item.title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Defines Quantum WalkScore (QWS), an application-oriented benchmark quantifying the largest problem size (n,d) on cycle and 2D-torus graphs where discrete-time quantum walks with amplitude amplification find a target node with measured success probability pexp(n,d)≥p∗(n,d) before first failure.

Grade 0.364 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Noé Olivier, Michel Nowak

Figure

Cycle and 2D-torus graph structures for nodefinding instances of sizes n=4 and n=3 with target nodes located at varied distances d from the source.

Asks

How can discrete-time quantum walks combined with amplitude amplification benchmark quantum computers on graph search problems?

But

Applies to gate-based quantum computers on cycle and 2D-torus graphs; walk step counts require 𝗇𝗎𝗆-𝗐≥d and 𝗇𝗎𝗆-𝗐≡d(mod2).

Tools

Discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) · Quantum amplitude amplification (AA) · IBM Heron r2, Heron r3, and Nighthawk r1 QPUs · Noiseless quantum circuit simulation

Abstract

Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

item.title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Reviews Suzuki-Trotter splitting methods, multi-product formulas, and alternative integrators for quantum time evolution, focusing on modern error-bound estimation and implementation trade-offs for noisy quantum hardware.

Grade 0.364 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “tensor network and matrix product state methods, and classical simulability of…” · Johann Ostmeyer

Asks

How do modern Suzuki-Trotter product formulas and alternative time-evolution algorithms perform, scale, and compare in practical quantum and classical simulations?

But

Mathematical proofs and low-level technical details omitted; pedagogical review oriented toward practical usage.

Tools

Suzuki-Trotter product formulas · multi-product formulas · quantum signal processing · time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) · symplectic integrators

Abstract

(Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.

item.arxave:abstract: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.
